## What it is

Forest managers learned that putting out every small fire lets fuel build up until a megafire burns everything. Gelman applies the lesson to science. For decades, criticism of published work was discouraged. Small "fires" such as critiques, failed replications and re-analyses were put out to protect reputations. That let a huge stock of fragile findings accumulate, and when the replication crisis came, it burned through whole literatures at once.

## Why it matters

Suppressing criticism doesn't prevent the reckoning. It postpones it and makes it larger. A steady flow of small corrections keeps the stock of vulnerable work low, so no single event threatens a whole field. The analogy argues for treating routine criticism and replication as healthy maintenance, the controlled burns of science, rather than as attacks.

## How it works

A toy model of fuel. Each year, new fragile findings are added to the stock. Small fires, meaning routine critiques, remove a fraction $s$ of the stock each year, and suppression lowers $s$. At an unpredictable time a crisis ignites and burns whatever stock has built up. The size of the crisis is the accumulated fuel, which is roughly the inflow divided by $s$ in steady state. Suppression makes it bigger.

## Simulated example

Watch the stock of fragile findings over 60 years under different levels of criticism suppression. A crisis strikes at a random year and burns the accumulated stock.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof suppression = Inputs.range([0, 0.98], {value: 0.85, step: 0.01, label: "Suppression of routine criticism"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 139, step: 1, label: "Random seed (timing of crisis)"})
```

```{ojs}
fire = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const crisisYear = r.int(30, 55);
  const run = (sup, label) => {
    let fuel = 10;
    return range(61).map(t => {
      let burned = 0;
      if (t === crisisYear) { burned = fuel; fuel = 0; }
      const row = {t, label, fuel, burned};
      fuel = fuel + 20 - fuel * 0.25 * (1 - sup);
      return row;
    });
  };
  return {crisisYear, rows: [...run(suppression, "Your suppression level"), ...run(0, "No suppression (controlled burns)")]};
}
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Replication and firefighting: suppressing small fires feeds a big one.
suppression <- 0.85 # suppression of routine criticism # <1>
set.seed(139) # <2>

crisis_year <- sample(30:55, 1) # when the crisis comes # <3>
run <- function(sup) {
  fuel <- 10
  path <- numeric(61)
  burned <- 0
  for (t in 0:60) {
    if (t == crisis_year) {
      burned <- fuel
      fuel <- 0
    }
    path[t + 1] <- fuel
    fuel <- fuel + 20 - fuel * 0.25 * (1 - sup) # criticism burns 25%/yr # <4>
  }
  list(path = path, burned = burned)
}
yours <- run(suppression)
open <- run(0)
cat("Crisis in year ", crisis_year, ": it burns ", round(yours$burned),
  " units of unexamined work with your suppression level, ",
  round(open$burned), " with none\n",
  sep = ""
)

matplot(0:60, cbind(yours$path, open$path), # <5>
  type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
  col = c("#d6604d", "#2166ac"), xlab = "Year",
  ylab = "Unexamined work (fuel)"
)
abline(v = crisis_year, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c(
  "Your suppression level",
  "No suppression (controlled burns)"
),
col = c("#d6604d", "#2166ac"), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
)
```
1. The page's control: how much routine criticism is suppressed.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. A replication crisis arrives at some point and burns all the unexamined work at once.
4. Each year new work arrives and routine criticism burns off a share of the backlog, unless it is suppressed.
5. Unexamined work over time. Suppressing the small fires lets the fuel build up for the big one.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# Replication and firefighting: suppressing small fires feeds a big one.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

suppression = 0.85  # suppression of routine criticism
rng = np.random.default_rng(139)

crisis_year = rng.integers(30, 56)  # when the crisis comes


def run(sup):
    fuel, path, burned = 10, [], 0
    for t in range(61):
        if t == crisis_year:
            burned, fuel = fuel, 0
        path.append(fuel)
        fuel = fuel + 20 - fuel * 0.25 * (1 - sup)  # criticism burns 25%/yr
    return path, burned


yours, burned_yours = run(suppression)
none, burned_none = run(0)
print(f"Crisis in year {crisis_year}: it burns {burned_yours:.0f} units of "
      f"unexamined work with your suppression level, {burned_none:.0f} "
      "with none")

plt.plot(yours, color="#d6604d", linewidth=2,
         label="Your suppression level")
plt.plot(none, color="#2166ac", linewidth=2,
         label="No suppression (controlled burns)")
plt.axvline(crisis_year, color="black", linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Unexamined work (fuel)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Suppressing routine criticism lets fragile findings pile up.
- Frequent small corrections prevent large, sudden collapses.
- Treat critiques and replications as maintenance, not as threats.
:::
